rv.q: So why five stars? Because it's so refreshing.

Writer Mike Bartlett has crafted an epic. Like his 2014 play King Charles III, The 47th is an imagination of a future world. The year is 2024, and Trump is having another bash at the presidency. But, while the play’s events feel eerie in their potential realism, Bartlett’s form is, crucially, theatrical.

'I know, I know, you hate me' declares the virtually unrecognisable Carvel at the outset, as he trundles on to Miriam Buether's sweeping thrust set in a golf cart. The 44-year-old actor is virtually half Trump's age, and yet the transformation is uncanny: there's the blonde wig and the fat suit, of ...
But it's gripping, funny, restless and ambitious, diving into the terrifying problem of leaders prepared to tear up democracy for their own ends.
Brilliant and witty, indisputably; but is it also insightful? Or does it simply recycle the usual wisdom about the irrational monster beyond the reach of the decent, omni-reasonable Democrats?
Bertie Carvel's Trump is alone worth the price of a ticket: not so much an impersonation as a reincarnation.
It's cartoonish fun, but it doesn't offer much more to chew on than a Spitting Image sketch.
Goold brings his usual sheen to proceedings, yet can't hide the lack of meaningful substance beneath the theatrical polish.

The result is fitfully brilliant and always utterly, utterly gripping, illuminated and irradiated by a central performance from Bertie Carvel that brings the 45th president to life with uncanny comic and chilling accuracy.
This is a performance that in itself makes this show worth seeing.
Bartlett is trying to have it both ways, but his twin styles are so at war with one another that they flatten both the intent and the content.
Carvel is the big draw here with another astonishing transformation...But as funny and compelling as the portrait is, it doesn’t tell us anything new.
It's a shame that this promising play is so detached from its subject-matter but the creative team have decided to write about US politics without reading about it.
A severe, intense lack of depth pervades the piece.

Inevitably, there is further civil unrest, led by the Shaman (Joss Carter), and Harris has to deal with the fallout. The political ambitions of Trump’s daughter Ivanka (Lydia Wilson, also superb) are ramped up by Bartlett – the consequences terrifying to contemplate.
It's a playful fever dream about the corrosive impact of populism and social media on democracy, featuring a grotesquely lifelike turn by Bertie Carvel as the orange-hued panto villain.
There's a perverse comedy to Trump and his interactions.
